speaker: Oriol Vinyals
title: No Priors Ep. 74 | With Google DeepMind VP of Research Oriol Vinyals
question: In frontier AI post-training, how can reward signals keep scaling once models surpass human expert performance?
guest: Traditionally, it's supervised learning—reward function means good or bad, so we can scale human annotation as much as we have so far. But I strongly believe there is a bootstrapping effect of models becoming better at judging their own outputs, and that really is maybe the main hypothesis of reinforcement learning as I see it. If checking that something is correct is easier than creating the solution, then we're in business because language models will be able to evaluate their own samples more accurately than they can generate them. Then we have a reinforcement learning loop because we can reinforce the ones that seem more promising, and the model gets better. Using the model itself as a reward—generative reward models—goes beyond the need for specific task annotations. We might still need some annotations, but the hope is that in the limit, you need only as many labels as a user would provide when teaching the system something new.

points.core: Checking an answer for correctness is fundamentally easier than generating it.
points.note: Accept: verification-generation asymmetry, evaluating outputs being simpler than producing solutions from scratch, or NP-style ease of checking. Do not credit: vague statements about self-improvement that omit why evaluation outpaces generation.

points.core: Models can bootstrap capability by evaluating their own generated candidate outputs.
points.note: Accept: generative reward models, LLM-as-a-judge scoring model samples, or reinforcing higher-rated self-generated rollouts in an RL loop. Do not credit: relying solely on human annotators or standard supervised fine-tuning.

points.core: Self-evaluating reward models reduce dependence on massive task-specific human label sets.
points.note: Accept: needing far fewer human annotations, moving beyond large labeled datasets, or needing only minimal user feedback for new tasks. Do not credit: claiming human feedback is completely unnecessary from day one.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Once models exceed human experts, reward can no longer come from humans directly judging outputs, so it has to shift toward signals that are cheaper to verify than to produce. The most robust source is ground truth that needs no human judgment: formal proof checkers, test suites, simulators, game outcomes, forecasts resolved by real events, and long-horizon task success in real or synthetic environments. Self-play and automatically generated curricula extend this, since an opponent or task generator that improves alongside the model keeps the difficulty at the frontier, as in AlphaZero.

Where no objective checker exists, the approach is to amplify limited human judgment rather than replace it: debate, critique and recursive decomposition let a weaker judge evaluate a stronger model by checking only small, verifiable pieces. Model-based graders, rubrics and constitutions written by experts, and learned reward models scale this further, with humans auditing samples instead of labeling everything.

The main limit is reward hacking: stronger models exploit flaws in any proxy, so graders must be hardened, ensembled and monitored as capability grows. Outside verifiable domains, this remains an open research problem.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Once models surpass human experts, post-training shifts from direct human labeling to exploiting the computational asymmetry between generation and verification. In formal and empirical domains, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards bypasses human ceilings by grounding feedback in objective oracles—such as code executors, formal proof assistants, scientific simulators, and real-world environment outcomes—where solutions remain cheap to check even when superhuman to discover. As static benchmarks saturate, asymmetric self-play sustains curriculum pressure by training generator policies to synthesize progressively harder, automatically verifiable problems.

In open-ended domains lacking deterministic verifiers, reward scaling relies on inference-time evaluation compute and scalable oversight. Generative reward models expend chain-of-thought reasoning, tool calls, and explicit rubrics to audit candidate responses, allowing evaluation quality to scale with test-time compute rather than unassisted human judgment. Meanwhile, protocols like AI debate, prover-verifier games, and recursive critique decompose complex, superhuman trajectories into narrow, localized claims that humans or ensembles of peer models can still adjudicate reliably, paired with adversarial red-teaming and uncertainty regularization to curb reward hacking as policy optimization intensifies.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Reward signals can keep scaling past human expert level if they stop relying on humans producing correct answers and lean on things that are easier to check than to create.

The strongest lever is verifiable rewards. Unit tests, proof checkers like Lean, simulators, compilers and real experimental results can grade work no human could produce, so reinforcement learning on these keeps working at any skill level. Where outcomes can't be checked mechanically, the field relies on the gap between judging and generating. Humans, or weaker models, can often reliably judge pieces of an answer, compare two answers, or check a critique, even when they couldn't write the answer themselves.

Scalable oversight methods build on that gap. Debate pits models against each other to expose flaws, recursive reward modeling splits hard tasks into steps a judge can assess, and AI-assisted critique helps human raters catch errors. Self-play and AI feedback let models produce harder tasks and grade them under constitutional rules, with checks for consistency.

The open risks are reward hacking and models gaming the grader. That's why robust verifiers, held-out evaluations and interpretability-based checks matter alongside these methods.

The most reliable source is verifiable, grounded feedback: in math, code, formal proofs, simulations, and real-world tool use, execution outcomes and formal verifiers provide objective rewards by exploiting the gap between generating a solution and checking it. In open-ended domains lacking automated verifiers, labs use scalable oversight—having AI systems decompose complex work into auditable steps, score against detailed rubrics, or debate one another—so weaker human or model judges can catch subtle flaws. Self-play and adversarial co-evolution further extend scaling by letting models generate progressively harder tasks, tests, and critiques for each other. Ultimately, keeping these signals trustworthy requires grounding proxy judges in real-world outcomes and continually refreshing evaluators to prevent reward hacking before models learn to game the verifier instead of improving.
